the old wrapper was foil with the color matching the flavor on the outside (yellow for bananna, etc.), and silver metallic color on the inside. the metallic wrapper could be gently unfolded first on the ends, and then along the middle to expose 100% of the marvelous, freshly broken taffy...and then folded back up and stuffed into your pocket!! very important for those quick getaways on your bike. (that might have had a bananna seat...)

this is my second "coffee-in-a-can" from illy issimo - my first being the much sweeter cappuccino.

i should preface my review by first saying that i am not a coffee drinker - i usually like my coffee in a dessert setting; being nice and sweet and creamy. i knew enough about coffees to know that the espresso would be the darker, more robust and more bitter of the two drinks, but wow - what a punch. i have been on a beer kick lately and many of the darker stout beers say that they have a strong "coffee flavor" which i never understood because i was expecting "coffee" as in the flavor i associate with something like coffee iced cream. after drinking this espresso drink, i now understand the flavor they talk about - and oddly enough, the first thought that came to my mind when i drank this was, "wow, this tastes like a beer." (not in the boozy sense, mind you - just the bitter bite and flavor overtones).

there is a twinge of sweetness to the drink, but nothing that i would consider having a major impact. the bitterness is pretty impressive considering that this small can has 10g of sugar - to put that into perspective, it has about half the sugar of a normal coke.

now... the caffeine part.

i don't really get much caffeine any more - i used to drink tons when i was a kid - going through multiple six-packs of coke in a week. nowadays the only caffeine i get is from iced tea at a restaurant (unsweet). so maybe it's because my tolerance is now a bit lower than it used to be, but this thing kicks like a mule. i drank the espresso about three hours after eating lunch, and i would say that i felt the impact within ten minutes of finishing off the can. it stuck with me for about an hour too. oddly enough, the cappuccino version of this drink took a few hours for me to feel the caffeine high. i checked out the can and found out why... pregnant women and people with heart issues should probably stay very far away from this drink.

here are some basic caffeine stats from the mayo clinic:
drink size caffeine
5-hour energy 2 oz. (60 ml) 207 mg
red bull 8.4 oz (250 ml) 76-80 mg
coca-cola classic 12 oz. (355 ml) 30-35 mg
mountain dew 12 oz. (355 ml) 46-55 mg

this little can is 6.8 fl oz (200ml) and contains 155 mg of caffeine.

if you're a big coffee drinker who takes a lot of their coffee strong and black, these numbers won't come as much of a shock to you since it's pretty much in line with normal brewed coffee. however, if you're no longer a caffeine junkie, don't be surprised if you suddenly feel the need to run a marathon.

my final verdict is that i like this stuff, although in the future i'd probably tend to stick more with the sweeter mochas and cappuccinos. if you're not a fan of the bitter coffees, i can't say i'd recommend this drink for you, but i didn't find the flavor as off-putting as many other reviewers seem to have.

i have been hearing about konjac noodles for the past couple of years and finally got around to trying them. they are actually not too bad, if you are looking for a high-fiber, low glycemic and zero-calorie food. i ate mine with marinara sauce and although it wasn't great, it wasn't that bad either. i agree with other reviewers that it would be better in asian dishes. i might try this instead of rice noodles in pancit (an epic filipino dish) or maybe pad thai. i have a really great recipe for a low-fat seafood alfredo but i just don't think the texture of these noodles (even the ribbon/fettuccine-like cut of konjac/shirataki noodles) would cut it for that dish.

to echo other reviewers: if you are sensitive to texture, you will probably have a hard time with konjac noodles. they can be rubbery. i think they are chewy and they remind me a little bit of calamari. i think konjac/shirataki noodles are a great thing f you are on a restricted diet, or if texture is something you can get used to.

the smell when i opened the package was not exactly palatable, but i soaked them in cold water, and rinsed them in the colander, and the smell completely went away.

all in all, even though the texture wasn't so rad, the plus side (calorie-free, carb-free, and high-fiber foodstuff to eat even if i've hit my daily allotment for food) definitely outweighs (heh, no pun intended) the downsides (chewiness, no taste) of the konjac/shirataki noodles. 4/5 stars.

table sugar is half fructose and half glucose. agave nectar is 95% fructose. refined fructose is about as toxic to your liver as alcohol. fructose can only be processed by the liver in a process that ends up creating uric acid (leads to gout), nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (cirrhosis similar to being an alcoholic), vldl cholesterol (the worst kind), increase your triglycerides, liver insulin resistance, blocks hormones (lectin) that tell you you're full, and cause hypertension due to it's diminishment of nitrous oxide in your blood (which is what lets you regulate your blood pressure). and, according to this film, 30% of the calories end up as fat. so - you take in fewer calories because it's sweeter, but end up storing a larger percentage as fat. and you end up hungrier in the long run, so - if it doesn't make you fat, the increase in appetite might.

their own faq does cover these topics, and as a counterpoint, they do mention fda studies that go along with fructose being safe, etc. [...] most of these are why i started looking into why people might be asking these questions of their products.

according to two other reviewers: "the taste is remarkably fresh for canned" and "the japanese would describe it as umami." i quite agree with both of these observations. some cautions, however:

you can't just open a can and eat it as if it were a can of sardines, or even a can of oil-pack tuna. the product is extremely oily -- in fact, it is 60% oil (richer than triple-creme brie)! it happens to be a healthful oil with vitamins a and d and omega 3 fats, but it is still a bit much. i compared the nutritional values to a somewhat smaller can of oil-packed sardines. the cod liver had less protein than one might expect -- 9 grams versus 16 for the sardines -- but off the chart on calories with 1165!

to make matters worse, the instructions on the can (if you can read them -- they're in four languages and the tiny print requires a strong magnifier to see) say, "must be consumed immediately after opening." i strongly suggest a skeptical regard to that. the "remarkably fresh" taste does change quickly even in the refrigerator, but the result is not unpleasant. a little fishier, perhaps. i kept some for over a week and it was still tasty.

by the way, you ought not to waste the oil. it is of course sold separately as cod liver oil and is a fine nutritional supplement.

so, i suggest a strategic approach to consuming a can. you don't want to eat it all at once (even if you have help), regardless of what the label says.

make no mistake... giving your dog raw foods, or dehydrated foods + rehydration, will beat all options. it is not really feasible for most people's lives and, even if it is feasible, its not easy to do at every treat time as well as meal time. the zero/g line from darford is the next best option. this includes their treats and food. my dogs love these shrimp/trout treats being reviewed. at 30 calories per treat its perfect for an active adult dog and easily breaks in half for smaller dogs with less caloric requirement and, of course, for lazy dogs.

this product probably should not be sub-named "with trout and shrimp". the first ingredient in this specific formula, mysis shrimp, is not a 'meal' and is not dry when measured. this means that after the 80% of water is taken out of the shrimp its true content would appear waaaay down the list of ingredients, possibly in the lower 25% of ingredients. the fourth ingredient, herring meal, is a legitimate measurement and gives this product most of its meat protein. the other meat included, trout, is not a meal nor dehydrated and is too far down the list to really even exist in the product. these treats would be more accurately sub-named "with herring", but i guess that isn't as appealing.

i would guess 45% of the protein in this treat is actually from meat, the rest from other ingredients especially peas.

a huge advantage of these treats, and the zero/g food, is the low glycemic effect on dogs. peas and buckwheat (which is a fruit, not a grain), and the other related ingredients in the product, have very little blood/sugar effect. so stop giving your dogs potatoes which will spike their glucose levels then cause them to come crashing down.

givin the price, these treats are a diamond in the rough!

maca powder = maca flour. i have cooked with maca flour ten years, as a baking and cooking ingredient/flavoring. in peru, maca flour, or "harina de maca" is a relatively cheap regional culinary flour. raw reform is a great specimen of this culinary flour; ideal for cooking, an excellent nutty flavor, it's bitterness subsiding with heat. a decade ago i could buy 'harina de maca' for $8/kg (and in peru, it's a mere $2-4/kg) - now i see this same inexpensive peruvian cooking flour sold as a "raw superfood" at an inflated price. it's very odd to have witnessed this metamorphosis.

the reason i gave this one star is simple - this company (among several others) suggests that you to eat this flour raw. like other cruciferous roots, maca can be particularly difficult to digest when raw. not only is it fiber-dense, it contains lots of goitrogenic compounds (a term which means 'thyroid-interfering,' not "goiter causing") - that's why the raw root and it's flour is so bitter - it's no wonder people have digestive issues and occasional hormonal (thyroid) complaints with raw maca. the one time i ate it raw, i experienced the stomachache, too! maca is dense in fiber and thyroid inhibiting/goitrogenic compounds (glucosinolates and isothyocyanates), both of which are lessened greatly or deactivated by heat. among the people who grow it, maca is not considered healthy unless cooked. it is therefore a great paradox that the "raw food" crowd has gotten hold of this vegetable that has always been, and by all accounts always should be cooked. this supplement is being backed by people whose basic food philosophy avoids the plant's very identity in human use. it would be like eating turnip flour, raw (except maca can even more bitter than this, in fact most of the lepidiums are). back into antiquity, maca has had to be cooked in order to be gentle on digestion, on metabolism, and it has been cooked traditionally for this purpose.

i have used the raw maca flour in cooking since 2002 where i first read about it in chris kilham's book "tales from the medicine trail" and began following an interest in this ancient food. i do use raw maca flour for cooking, baking, in pancakes, confections, etc. where you can get it inexpensively, it is excellent for such uses. for therapeutic effects and everyday drink mix usage, presently i employ a 'black gelatinized' maca - it seems to be the strongest type energetically and for sexual effects, and 'black root' is my personal preference. 'gelatinized' means that it's fiber has been removed (skimmed off), and goitrogens denatured - it is a few times concentrated over the powder / flour. naturally, it is less bitter than any uncooked flour product. the gelatinized processing was developed specifically to address the digestion/goitrogen issue inherent with the root. that's the process' entire purpose - that's why it even exists.

the trend in "health food" circles says to eat maca raw, in order to glean the mood, stamina, and sexual benefits which andean people have known for thousands of years. these merchants never mention how the plant has always been prepared - cooked - perhaps the most crucial aspect of it's identity. why argue from antiquity about all the health benefits, while ignoring the food's ethnobotany? it's a mix of mistaken understanding, and because there's profit in re-selling a highly marked up culinary flour. i see $20.00 - $25.00 a pound slapped on maca flour in health food stores -- on a product which can be found $2-4 a kilogram in peru ($1.36 - $1.81/lb!). this is precisely why some regional foods / surpluses suddenly become "superfoods." in maca's case there is a genuine positive effect being felt... so, like the mood boost one feels with coffee, maca is an easy sell. most companies have a whole marketing song & dance... and they make a lot of money.

pay a price of $20/lb only for the gelatinized product, which has actually been processed for immediate consumption. do not pay this for a re-packed culinary flour.

each "retriever roll" is an inch and a quarter in diameter, and just shy of 10" in length. there are 2 rolls per package. zoey chewed on one of these last night for about half an hour and maybe only took off an inch or inch and a half of the retriever roll. each roll lasts through six 30-minute chewing sessions for zoey. in comparison, zoey could go through an entire 5" long dingo dyno stick in half an hour, and dyno stix only come 3 to a pkg for roughly the same price as two jumbo wag'n wraps. i believe the jumbo wag'n wraps are a better deal, and i store the partially chewed wag'n wrap in a large ziploc bag for the next evening's chewing session.

when you first look at the end of a wag'n wrap, it looks like it's a single layer of rawhide over a thick meaty center. this would be too easy for my dog to chew through. i'm glad to say that there are many layers of rawhide to this treat, and that the meaty part appears to run in a thin strip down the middle of the roll, with some of the meaty mixture thinly spread between the rawhide layers. much more difficult for zoey to chew through, but she still gets the meaty satisfaction.

let me first start by saying we are not gluten free because we have to be. we are gluten free by choice. i made this cake to try at accommodating some family members that are gluten free.

i bought this starter-starter 16 months ago and forgot about it. i started the starter about eight months ago. i followed the directions pretty faithfully. it didn't seem really active and i never used it. i've stored in in the refrigerator since then. i try to feed it every two weeks but sometimes it stretches in to a month. if it goes past two weeks, a lot of "hooch" collects on the top. i just pour it off, throw away half of the mix and add 1/4 cup of flour, 2 oz. of filtered water, mix it up and let it stand covered overnight before returning it to the refrigerator the next morning. it is obviously "active".
i actually started using it about four months ago, making schlotzky buns; supplementing with a little yeast. it works fine.
then i used it in no-knead bread, again supplementing it with a little yeast. it made fine bread, but not sour, at all.
finally, i went all in and made no-knead using the starter as the only leavening. it made a wonderful loaf. it is very flavorful and truly "sour" tasting. it rivals the sourdoughs of sf and i lived there for 12 years.

the recipe involves activating some starter over night, making the dough and letting it rise over night. refrigerating it 1-3 days to autolyze, then making the loaf, letting it rise another 3 hours and finally bake.

as you can see, this recipe requires really thinking ahead if you don't make it every day.

for me, it wasn't a quick and easy path to authentic sf sourdough, but in the end it turned out to be just what i was hoping for.

yea, those who claim these bars are not "real" pemmican are right. the original stuff was a mix of dried beef and rendered fat, sometimes with whatever local berries could be found. even those who ate it regularly hated it. (mostly voyagers and the like.)

better by far were the old wilson meat bars of the early '70s. the us military still uses something similar in some of their mres. sadly i can find no source for the bars any more.

3. bewitched, bothered and bewildered - a criminal mastermind unites four thieves to rip off a package from a shipping company...but not even the suspects know who arranged the crime or why.

(disc 2)
4. why can't you behave - a senator's plane crashes, and the case becomes personal for mccabe when he learns his own son may have supplied faulty parts to the airline.
5. poor butterfly - when a ruthless pimp savagely punishes one of his prostitutes, jake and mccabe vow to get him off the streets.
6. it ain't necessarily so - while breaking-and-entering, a panicked thief shoots the wife of an adult magazine publisher....or that just might be the cover story for a more sinister crime.
7. someone to watch over me - an apparent case of a drug overdose reveals unexpected complications when the victim's dealer becomes the target of a mysterious shooter.

(disc 3)
8. they can't take that away from me - after jake's planned bust of a drug-for-guns deal goes awry, two cops from the team wind up dead in an apparent retaliatory strike.
9. side by side - when a gang leader blows up a fishing boat, mccabe ends up stranded on an isolated island, while his friends fear that he's dead.
10. snow fall - when one of jake's informants winds up dead in a sting operation, he vows to catch the counterfeiter responsible for her death.

i had to smile at a previous review noting that what the reviewer liked best about this product is the packaging. yes, the packaging is brilliant -- well thought out, and deftly executed in an appealing orangey-peach, or maybe a peachy orange. this is one i'll definitely recycle and re-use, after removing the product and the label.

ah, the label. that's the first problem. (no, actually, that's the *second* problem. because if you're a manufacturer and you hear customers raving about the packaging rather than about the product, you know you might have a bigger problem than labeling.)

as for the label, the information it provides appears to be accurate. yes, a quarter-teaspoonful of nectresse certainly provides the sweetness of a teaspoon of sugar. with that sweetness, though, comes a bit of an aftertaste -- not terrible, but present. add a second quarter-teaspoonful to the first, however, and what you get is --for me, at least -- an undrinkable cup of coffee with a conspicuous aftertaste, a bowl of oatmeal so excessively sweet as to be off-putting. for me, the degree of aftertaste seems to depend on the food into which the nectresse is blended: a quarter-spoonful in a 16-ounce glass of iced tea was not unpleasant. more than that, as in coffee and oatmeal, was too much for me. a quarter-teaspoon in a half-cup of high-end, strongly flavored greek yogurt, however, changed my initial two-star rating to three; in some preparations, i could learn to like this product.

for some users, the more disturbing aspect of the label is the ingredients list. as noted above, the second ingredient (meaning the second-largest quantity in the formulation of the product) is sugar; the fourth, molasses. the presence of sugar (or molasses) in any food product is, for those of us who have had gastric bypass or other digestive procedures or issues, is a red flag (try googling "dumping syndrome" if you're not sure what happens when many or most who've had gastric bypass consume sugar in even small quantities). the amount of sugar in nectresse is said to be very small indeed, but i feel way more comfortable with splenda's list of ingredients: maltodextrin and sucralose. while both splenda and nectresse are derived from sugar, i am inclined to stick with the former, which i know my body can tolerate without unhappy consequences.

10/20/12 - after trying this product in various foods over the past couple of weeks, i've come to like it better and added a star. my earlier impressions still stand, however: used sparingly (and i do mean sparingly) and selectively, choosing those foods in which it works for me and those in which it doesn't, i've come to believe this is a worthwhile product with some promise in the marketplace. a neighbor who tried it along with me liked it a great deal, but we -- both long-time, regular users of splenda -- wondered why nectresse would ever replace splenda (with its handy teaspoon-for-teaspoon equivalency to sugar) on our shelves. on the table, maybe. but in the pantry? i'm still not sure.

after several issues including cracked nipples, poor latch, problems pumping, and a fussy baby i decided to start to ween at 3 weeks. by the time she was 4 weeks old i was down to two nursing sessions a day and supplementing with formula for the rest. then, as i healed and felt less stress about nursing the whole process got easier so i decided to try to increase my nursing/pumping sessions and decrease her formula intake. unfortunately, by that point i could only pump 1/4 ounce per breast and she was easily taking in 3 ounces per session with the bottle. i ordered a case of this tea and took the recommended dosage for 2 weeks without success. then i tried increasing the dose to two bags at a time, 4 times a day. you do have to take the time to steep it corectly (10 minutes, covered). i saw minimal results after increasing the dosage which could have also been attributed to increasing the number of pumping sessions or additional water intake per day rather than the tea. if you're used to herbal teas you probably won't mind the taste too much. it's rather nice with a bit of milk and honey added in. it does smell faintly of black licorice, but i never noticed it in the flavor. after i finished off the case of tea i tried fenugreek capsules and saw a bit better improvement in supply (an additional 2-3 ounces per day). i can now pump about 4-6 ounces a day (up from a total of 2 ounces a day when i first started) while i'm at work and i nurse her at the start of every feeding at home. i still need to supplement with formula since she'll now take in between 4-6 ounces at a time at 3 months old. i wish i was one of the lucky ones to see an increase of 6-8 ounces per feeding/pumping session, but i'm happy that i was able to bring my supply back as much as i have. now i'm combining blessed thistle with fenugreek to see if i can get any additional output. 15 pills a day has been challenging for me, particularly since i'm not the best at swallowing them. i'm trying to hang on to my supply, as low as it may be, as long as i can though. so, for me it's worth it. definitely give the tea a try if you're having trouble with supply, but just know that it has such low doses of the herbs that it isn't effective for everyone. if you don't have success with the tea it's worth trying out fenugreek and blessed thistle too.

i had been waking up every morning to see as many as 6 squirrels happily frolicking in my backyard. didn't see this as much of a problem until they worked their way onto my roof and into every open cavity in my house. sealing these openings didn't eliminate their presence entirely. cutting back tree access worked to some extent, but the ones who really wanted to get back on the roof would ultimately find a way.

shortly after discovering that my gutter had become a nesting area for the squirrels, i declared war on the critters, and picked up both the critter ridder spray and granules. i generously applied the granules to the roof and gutter areas, and the spray to the trunks of all the trees that they would frequent.

the next morning, there were no signs of squirrels anywhere near my house. sure, my trees smelled of pepper for a day or two, but the critter ridder worked in helping me relocate these little buggers to someone else's yard.

will it work for your raccoon problems? - no idea. but it did send my squirrels to another, more-welcoming, part of town. and when one returns, a healthy reapplication of the spray seems to get rid of them for another few weeks.

gelatin takes twice as long to dissolve when used with cream or milk.

ensuring the smooth texture of a finished product.
it involves sprinkling the powdered gelatin into a liquid

a baby food recall just issued by the fda (jan. 2010) may have some of the most stomach-churning details i've read in awhile:

"swollen or leaking pouches may indicate problems with the product, including possible contamination by bacteria that can cause illness, or that the packaging has been compromised and is at risk of bacterial contamination."

the recalled food is made by happy baby, and it's a mix of the baby and toddler lines that parents should be throwing out. the recall covers:

* happytot green bean, pear & peas, net wt. 4.22 oz. (120g), upc 8 52697 00127 9;
* happytot sweet potato, carrot, apple & cinnamon, net wt. 4.22 oz. (120g), upc 8 52697 00128 6;
* happytot spinach, mango & pear, net wt. 4.22 oz. (120g), upc 8 52697 00129 3;
* happytot butternut squash & apple, net wt. 4.22 oz. (120g), upc 8 52697 00130 9;
* happytot banana, peach, coconut & prunes, net wt. 4.22 oz. (120g), upc 8 52697 00131 6;
* happytot banana, peach & mango, net wt. 4.22 oz. (120g), upc 8 52697 00132 3
* happybaby mango, net wt. 3.5 oz. (99g), upc 8 52697 00134 7
* happybaby spinach mango pear, net wt. 3.5 oz. (99g), upc 8 52697 00139 2
* happybaby apricot sweet potato, net wt. 3.5 oz. (99g), upc 8 52697 00136 1

the foods are sold in plastic pouches with plastic caps, and none are set to expire until late this year or even next year, so check through the stuff way back on your shelf. no illnesses have been reported so far, and happy baby's ceo shazi isram said in a company statement that this is a voluntary precautionary recall.

if your pouches are leaking or swollen, the fda advises you keep them away not just from baby but from your pets as well and wash your hands if you've handled the packages.

happy baby directs parents to return them to the store for a full refund or contact them at 718-852-7606 or info@happybabyfood.com

kraft mac and cheese veggie pasta boasts a half serving of vegetables per serving of mac and cheese. they accomplish this sneaky feat by incorporating cauliflower into the macaroni. while i do have opinions on the long-term benefits of disguising vegetables into kids' food as opposed to feeding them actual vegetables, i will put my concerns aside in an effort to objectively review this product. (besides, mac and cheese is a highly processed food anyway, which leads to a whole other debate).

without comparing ingredient lists (which i prefer not to look at for this type of food), it appears that the characteristic cheese sauce pouch has been unaltered. the orange, salty yet creamy taste that i loved as a child and as an adult is intact. the only issue i had with the veggie version is the macaroni texture. the traditional kraft macaroni is forgiving as far as cooking times - i have overcooked and undercooked the macaroni over the years with acceptable results. however, though i followed the cooking time guidelines and tasted the noodles frequently, the overall texture was somewhat mushy compared to the traditional recipe.

in order to get a whole serving of vegetables, one would have to eat the whole box of mac and cheese (which is something i have certainly done). clearly this product is not satisfy the "strive for 5 fruits and vegetables a day" criteria for healthy eating, but i suppose that it is better than nothing. because lets face it - kraft mac and cheese is good, and people old and young are going to eat it anyway, so why not have half a serving of cauliflower at the same time?

having worked in the canned seafood industry, i sampled this product at work for consistency, quality, and taste. it was excellent back in 2007. i soon relied on this product for lunch (with ritz crackers, genova tonno was very, very good) and also sometimes for snacks. i'd buy them in bulk here on amazon at reasonable prices.

having worked with canned tuna, i can tell you the prices of the "commodity" have gone way up across the board for light tuna (e.g. skipjack) and white tuna (e.g. albacore). this is due to increased fishing cost and decreased supply of fish. as sad of an issue as overfishing due to the trawling methods, the reality is we're seeing this reflected in the cost and quality of various seafood products, most notably via the traditional 6oz cans being downsized to 5oz first by starkist followed by other shelf stable seafood manufacturers.

so this genova tonno product used to be chunks of tuna in extra virgin olive oil with a nice balanced amount of salt. however, this product is now watery chunky tuna that has a bit of olive oil in it. and in case you didn't know, genova is owned by chicken of the sea, who is actually owned by a thai based company called thai union, which has its own packing facilities in thailand. this is not italian tuna, do not let the name fool you. it is italian-style, and like most of chicken of the sea products, genova tonno is packed in thailand. genova products are still very good and of a decent quality, but it just is not what it used to be because of the rising costs.

given the higher prices of this product, i no longer recommend this due to the $2+ per 3oz can price tag. this used to make for a relatively healthy, affordable and delicious lunch or snack, but it is now not a very good value. i recommend other alternatives (skip the pre-made canned tuna spread, it's got too much mayo and salt in it). or consider making your own tonno/olive oil tuna. just try and look for "natural" tuna if you can since trusted brands' old fashioned canned tuna in water contains vegetable broth/hydrolized protein that is injected to allow the fish to soak up more water (industry's dirty little secret). there are plenty of fast and easy to prepare tuna/salmon options online if you look close hard enough on amazon...

i was crestfallen. with the exception of hot chocolate or a chai latte, i don't like sweetened drinks at all. i love sweet foods, but not sweet beverages. once, in a restaurant, i was served sweetened ice tea. i didn't know it had sugar in it, and i nearly spit it out on the table. in a word, yuck! so i wasn't looking forward to trying this.
